UPDATE: 1 BILLION RAND HOUSING NORTHERN CAPE

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A year after the Premier’s billion-rand promise, the people of the Northern Cape are still waiting no houses, no hope, just politics built on empty ground.

Unique Selling Point:
Before the elections, the ANC promised change again but in the Northern Cape, not a single brick has been laid, and the only thing still standing are the lies.

Summary:
In April 2024, Carte Blanche visited the Northern Cape to investigate broken infrastructure and undelivered promises in towns across the province.
Among the voices that defined that story was Nellie Frans, a 55-year resident of a shanty settlement outside Kimberley, who told us she had been waiting her entire life for a proper home.
During that interview, we confronted Premier Zamani Saul about the stalled R1 billion housing project announced only months earlier. Standing on a sewage-drenched street, he assured Carte Blanche that “by the end of the month, a contractor will be putting up site there.”

Eighteen months later, nothing has happened.
The community says no contractor ever arrived, no foundations have been dug, and no houses are planned for the site where the Premier made his pledge. Residents claim that the few housing allocations that have gone ahead in Leratoville have been politically selective — allegedly limited to ANC-aligned individuals — and that the newly built houses there are structurally unsound, with cracks, collapsing walls, and poor finishes.
For people like Nellie Frans, who once believed that promise might finally bring change, the disillusionment has deepened.

Further information:
In April 2024, Carte Blanche visited the Northern Cape to investigate broken infrastructure and undelivered promises in towns across the province.
Among the voices that defined that story was Nellie Frans, a 55-year resident of a shanty settlement outside Kimberley, who told us she had been waiting her entire life for a proper home.

During that interview, we confronted Premier Zamani Saul about the stalled R1 billion housing project announced only months earlier. Standing on a sewage-drenched street, he assured Carte Blanche that “by the end of the month, a contractor will be putting up site there.”

Eighteen months later, nothing has happened.
The community says no contractor ever arrived, no foundations have been dug, and no houses are planned for the site where the Premier made his pledge. Residents claim that the few housing allocations that have gone ahead in Leratoville have been politically selective — allegedly limited to ANC-aligned individuals — and that the newly built houses there are structurally unsound, with cracks, collapsing walls, and poor finishes.

For people like Nellie Frans, who once believed that promise might finally bring change, the disillusionment has deepened.

⸻

STORY FOCUS / ANGLE

The follow-up revisits Nellie and her community to ask one simple question:
Did the Premier keep his promise?

We return to the site where the R1 billion housing project was unveiled to find out:
• Has construction begun?
• Were tenders issued or funds allocated?
• Who, if anyone, received houses?
• Are housing allocations being politicised?
• And what has become of the Premier’s public assurance that “by the end of the month” work would start?

KIMBERLEY: 1 BILLION RAND HOUSING FINAL SCRIPT

OPENING
UPSOUND
GOVAN WHITTLES: “Ag allright, allright, vir die mense by die huis wat nie weet nie, hierdie is my antie Nellie van die Noord Kaap van die Roodepan…
Ah, all right, all right — for the people at home who don’t know, this is my aunt Nellie from the Northern Cape, from Roodepan…
GOVAN WHITTLES: We’ve returned to a small house in Roodepan, outside Kimberley, where we met Nellie Frans just before last year’s elections. It was around the time President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a one-billion-rand housing project in the area.

NELLIE FRANS: Die president het gesê hier kom staan ‘n hospitaal en ‘n skool.
The president said a hospital and a school would be built here.
GOVAN WHITTLES: An undertaking Northern Cape Premier, Zamani Saul, assured us last April they would fulfil.
PREMIER ZIMANI SAUL: “I’m certain by the end of the month, a contractor would put up site there”.
NELLIE FRANS: Toe julle hier weg is, nee toe kom die mense, toe kom daar ‘n TLB, toe gaan maak hulle skoon toe sien ons hier is ‘n verandering.
When you left, people came with a TLB, they cleaned around here and we could see change is coming.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Toe wat het hulle opgesit?
What did they erect here?
NELLIE FRANS: Toe maak hulle eers die kamp, toe kom daai dik swaar yster, ek weet nie wat is daai nie, ‘n containertjie. Toe sit hulle daai op.
They first made a camp, then a thick black iron thing, I think it’s a container, they put that up.
GOVAN WHITTLES: A year-and-a-half later, Nellie’s dream of a house remains just that, a fenced-off container and wooden shed. But she’s still hopeful.

SOURCE: A001C006_2510144C
00:04:37:19
GOVAN: Dink my antie julle gaan iets kry?
Do you think you’re gonna get something?
00:04:43:06
NELLIE FRANS: Ek glo ek gaan kry, hulle kan ons nie empty blik maak nie, uh uh
I believe I’m going to get, yes, I’m going to get., they can’t make us empty cans, then I will have to call you again.

GOVAN WHITTLES: But even if government delivers on this promise, it’ll mean little for as long as Kimberley’s Sol Plaatje Municipality drowns in its own neglect.

DR HENK BOSHOFF: “30 Years into democracy and people are living like animals”

GOVAN WHITTLES: While we were in the area, the Human Rights Commission was there too, probing governance in the province.

DR HENK BOSHOFF: I want to put it on record and I hope they are watching. The provincial government, cannot just overlook what is happening in this municipality, its nonsense. 3’43’03” Good grief man,

ELSPETH KHWINANA: Why should you not be criminally charged and in fact be removed from office.

GOVAN WHITTLES: last time we were here a year ago, there was sewage running in the streets where the premier stays, that seems to have been cleared up but if you thought that was bad, wait till you see what we discovered this time.
FADE

ACT 1
UPSOUND: PEOPLE GATHERING AND GREETING EACH OTHER
GOVAN WHITTLES: In Platfontein, Khwe is still spoken as a mother tongue, the only place where the language continues to passed down.
UPSOUND
GOVAN WHITTLES: Their village lies barely ten minutes from the Premier’s house.
BREATHE AND LET US SEE HIM IN THE CHURCH
GOVAN WHITTLES: Village elder Josef Kajanga preserves the stories of his people, including their place as South Africans.
JOSEF KAJANGA: Ek is gebore in Angola. Ek is ‘n Khwe. Ek is nie gemeng na ‘n ander ras nie, ek is ‘n Kwe, uitgestaan, geskape deur God.

I was born in Angola.I am Khwe. I am not mixed with any other race, I am Khwe, distinct, created by God

VO: Known for their tracking skills, the Khwe served in militaries across Southern Africa, a role that saw them forced from Angola to Namibia, before the South African Defence Force resettled them at the former army base in Schmidtsdrift, near Kimberley.

JOSEF KAJANGA: Spoorsny word nie geleer nie, jy leer hom van kleins af. Ons het ook mekaar geken se spoor, ons eie mense se spoor wat hy getrap is ook geken. Ons het nie skoene gehad nie so ek kan ken wie hier getrap en geloop het, dan sê ek hier geloop Jan, of daar geloop Jacob. As jy het my goed gevat dan ken ek, oh, Jan het my goed kom vat hierso. Ek sny hom tot by sy huis.
Tracking cant be taught, you learn it from childhood. We also knew each other’s tracks, our own people’s tracks that had been walked, we knew them too. We didn’t have shoes so I can tell who walked here, then I say “Jan walked here,” or “Jacob walked there.” If he took my things then I know, “oh, Jan took my things from here.” I track him all the way to his house.

GOVAN WHITTLES: In 2003, Nelson Mandela granted the Khwe their own farm, a place they could finally call home. Markus Jetembo is one of the community leaders.
MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons lewe van ploeg, so hierdie was ‘n gedeelte wat skoon land gewees het en droogland gewees het. Dit was eintlik geskik vir ons om te ploeg.
We were very happy when we got the place, Platfontein. And we had hoped because our people’s history tells that we live from farming, that this land, which was open and dry, would be a good place for us to cultivate.
GOVAN WHITTLES: On farmland meant to preserve their culture, Markus shows us a lake that has formed here over the past seven years. At first, it appears to be a serene stretch of water until he tells us it’s a dam entirely filled with sewage, dumped here by the Sol Plaatje Municipality.
GOVAN WHITTLES: I’ve covered sewage in the streets all over the country and I’ve seen what dilapidated sewage plants looks like, but this is unlike anything I’ve ever seen.
GOVAN WHITTLES: And it keeps expanding, yet Platfontein doesn’t even have a sewage network.
MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons wat nie dienste kry nie, ons wat nie flush toilette het nie, hoekom sal rioolwater by onse plaas gegooi word?
We’re the ones who don’t get services, who don’t even have flush toilets, so why would sewage be dumped on our land?
GOVAN WHITTLES: Markus says they’re treated like the sewage on their land, cast aside by government because of who they are.

MARKUS JETEMBO: Die oudtydse regering het mos ons ouers gebruik gemaak om hulle te help veg. Dit is hoekom hierdie SuidAfrika sien vir ons as vreemdelinge en vir ons nie die nodige dienste wil gee nie.
The old government used our parents to fight alongside them. That’s why this South Africa sees us as foreigners and doesn’t want to give us the services we need.
GOVAN WHITTLES: But the mess on their land isn’t isolated, it’s just a symptom of an entire network in freefall.

TUMELO MOSIKARI: This is Goga pumpstation, it’s where the sewage from Galeshewe comes from, Galeshewe, Carter’s glen and all the other high lying areas comes to.
VO: In Galeshewe, Kimberley’s largest township, activist Tumelo Mosikari visits the pump station often and tells us the pumps haven’t been switched on for a long time.

GOVAN WHITTLES: What are we gonna see if we go in here?
TUMELO MOSIKARI: A non-functioning pumpstation that has had millions allocated to it’s upgrade.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Ok, let me ask first.
GOVAN WHITTLES: The supervisor appears from the parking lot, insisting the pumps are working.
GOVAN WHITTLES: We just want to see if the pumpstation is working,
SHAYLE GREY: Ja, it is working. I just came from there. I just came from there and I switched it off now.
Govan: you just switched it off now?
SHAYLE GREY: I’m actually on my way to go start it again.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Inside, the only sign of repair or maintenance we see is a few railings being painted.

SHAYLE GREY There was a lot of stories you know that you can venture into and stuff like that, there was complications at Goga pumpstation, but we fixed it.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Inside the main system where raw sewage is meant to be pumped out, it’s clear nothing’s working; the water lies still, and one pump is missing. The pump is switched on while we film. But less than ten minutes later, it’s switched off again. Construction work on the pipeline is given as the reason for the sudden shutdown.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Shayle has just switched the pump off and now this plant is back to not working. It’s clear they only switched it on for us.
GOVAN WHITTLES: We know the only reason they switched it off so quickly was to keep us from seeing it bubbling out, just beyond the wall, in an open field next to the station.

GOVAN WHITTLES: have you ever seen anything like this, a sewage river, a manmade sewage river, with banks.
TUMELO MOSIKARI: No, and this is normal, this is not something that happened last year. This is pre-2018. In 2018 there was a 30 million Rand project to upgrade the facility.
GOVAN WHITTLES: and where did that money go?
TUMELO MOSIKARI: Probably down the drain as well.
GOVAN WHITTLES: Has this sewage river ever stopped running since 2018?
TUMELO MOSIKARI: No, it’s never stopped running, if it had stopped running there wouldn’t be a lake.
VO: The sewage river runs for several kilometres and then passes under a provincial road to finally end up in Platfontein. Last year, we reported how the provincial government spent 30 million Rand to raise a part of this road over the sewage instead of fixing the problem.
GOVAN WHITTLES: This place is appropriately called the Zamani Soul sewage lake, because this will be the premier’s legacy. It’s a monument of disgust and dysfunction.

JOSEF KAJANGA: Die provinsiale regering sê daar is nie geld genoeg om vir julle spoeltoilette te kan maak nie. Daar is nie geld om vir julle die krag te kan aanlê nie om vir julle die waterlyn te kan aanlê nie.
The provincial government says there isn’t enough money to give you flush toilets. There’s no money to bring you electricity, or to install water lines.
MARKUS JETEMBO: Ek het self by die human rights commission gaan complain oor die feit dat die munisipalteit vir ons bill maar ons kry nie enige diens van die munisipalteit by ons nie.
I personally went to the Human Rights Commission to complain about the fact that the municipality bills us, but we don’t receive any services from them.
GOVAN WHITTLES: The municipality struggled to explain why Platfontein is being billed at all.
SOL PLAATJE: “Im not 100% sure, because from my understanding, there is toilets, which means they are getting water from us, so that means we must bill them”
MARKUS JETEMBO : Ons het nie flush toilette nie.
We don’t have flush toilets
GOVAN WHITTLES: Hulle sê julle het.
They say you do.
MARKUS JETEMBO : Julle sal net droog saksisteme kry by ons.
You’ll only find dry bagging systems here.
GOVAN WHITTLES: When the Human Rights Commission pressed the municipal leadership for answers, they were left dumbstruck, unable to explain even the basics.

UPSOUND SOL PLAATJE: We cant drink water from the tap is that the question, maybe I misunderstood the questions, maybe I’ll give the question to someone

ELSBETH KHWINANA: COMMISSIONER: You don’t even understand why you are in that seat.
DR HENK BOSHOFF: This session was an embarrassment for the Sol Plaatje municipality. It is clear that its administration does not know what to do.
GOVAN WHITTLES: The commission will push for the report to reach Parliament, something the Khwe hope will finally see them recognised.

MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons is mense wat nou nog met ons tradisie sit en ons tradisie praktiseer. Hoe gaan ons ons Vryheid geniet? Ons voel nie deel van SuidAfrika nie, ons voel geïsoleerd.
We are people who still practice our traditions. How will we enjoy our freedom. We don’t feel part of South Africa, we feel isolated

Raw sewage is coming from the community, its supposed to be pumped to where its treated, its not being treated. Instead of pumping it here they have opened a manhole in the veld to let the raw sewage out. This raw sewage created a lake in Platfontein next to the R31.

TUMELO MOSIKARI

They work here, they get paid to make sure that this doesn’t happen and it has been happening for years.

TIMELINE PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO
In Kimberley, one of South Africa’s last indigenous communities finds itself at odds with the municipality, fighting not just neglect, but erasure.

It was around the time President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a one-billion-rand housing project in the area. NELLIE FRANS: Die president het gesê hier kom staan ‘n hospitaal en ‘n skool. The president said a hospital and a school would be built here. GOVAN WHITTLES: An undertaking Northern Cape Premier, Zamani Saul, assured us last April they would fulfil. PREMIER ZIMANI SAUL: “I’m certain by the end of the month, a contractor would put up site there”. NELLIE FRANS: Toe julle hier weg is, nee toe kom die mense, toe kom daar ‘n TLB, toe gaan maak hulle skoon toe sien ons hier is ‘n verandering. When you left, people came with a TLB, they cleaned around here and we could see change is coming. GOVAN WHITTLES: Toe wat het hulle opgesit? What did they erect here? NELLIE FRANS: Toe maak hulle eers die kamp, toe kom daai dik swaar yster, ek weet nie wat is daai nie, ‘n containertjie. Toe sit hulle daai op. They first made a camp, then a thick black iron thing, I think it’s a container, they put that up. GOVAN WHITTLES: A year-and-a-half later, Nellie’s dream of a house remains just that, a fenced-off container and wooden shed. But she’s still hopeful. SOURCE: A001C006_2510144C 00:04:37:19 GOVAN: Dink my antie julle gaan iets kry? Do you think you’re gonna get something? 00:04:43:06 NELLIE FRANS: Ek glo ek gaan kry, hulle kan ons nie empty blik maak nie, uh uh I believe I’m going to get, yes, I’m going to get., they can’t make us empty cans, then I will have to call you again. GOVAN WHITTLES: But even if government delivers on this promise, it’ll mean little for as long as Kimberley’s Sol Plaatje Municipality drowns in its own neglect. DR HENK BOSHOFF: “30 Years into democracy and people are living like animals” GOVAN WHITTLES: While we were in the area, the Human Rights Commission was there too, probing governance in the province. DR HENK BOSHOFF: I want to put it on record and I hope they are watching. The provincial government, cannot just overlook what is happening in this municipality, its nonsense. 3’43’03” Good grief man, ELSPETH KHWINANA: Why should you not be criminally charged and in fact be removed from office. GOVAN WHITTLES: last time we were here a year ago, there was sewage running in the streets where the premier stays, that seems to have been cleared up but if you thought that was bad, wait till you see what we discovered this time. FADE ACT 1 UPSOUND: PEOPLE GATHERING AND GREETING EACH OTHER GOVAN WHITTLES: In Platfontein, Khwe is still spoken as a mother tongue, the only place where the language continues to passed down. UPSOUND GOVAN WHITTLES: Their village lies barely ten minutes from the Premier’s house. BREATHE AND LET US SEE HIM IN THE CHURCH GOVAN WHITTLES: Village elder Josef Kajanga preserves the stories of his people, including their place as South Africans. JOSEF KAJANGA: Ek is gebore in Angola. Ek is ‘n Khwe. Ek is nie gemeng na ‘n ander ras nie, ek is ‘n Kwe, uitgestaan, geskape deur God. I was born in Angola.I am Khwe. I am not mixed with any other race, I am Khwe, distinct, created by God VO: Known for their tracking skills, the Khwe served in militaries across Southern Africa, a role that saw them forced from Angola to Namibia, before the South African Defence Force resettled them at the former army base in Schmidtsdrift, near Kimberley. JOSEF KAJANGA: Spoorsny word nie geleer nie, jy leer hom van kleins af. Ons het ook mekaar geken se spoor, ons eie mense se spoor wat hy getrap is ook geken. Ons het nie skoene gehad nie so ek kan ken wie hier getrap en geloop het, dan sê ek hier geloop Jan, of daar geloop Jacob. As jy het my goed gevat dan ken ek, oh, Jan het my goed kom vat hierso. Ek sny hom tot by sy huis. Tracking cant be taught, you learn it from childhood. We also knew each other’s tracks, our own people’s tracks that had been walked, we knew them too. We didn’t have shoes so I can tell who walked here, then I say “Jan walked here,” or “Jacob walked there.” If he took my things then I know, “oh, Jan took my things from here.” I track him all the way to his house. GOVAN WHITTLES: In 2003, Nelson Mandela granted the Khwe their own farm, a place they could finally call home. Markus Jetembo is one of the community leaders. MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons lewe van ploeg, so hierdie was ‘n gedeelte wat skoon land gewees het en droogland gewees het. Dit was eintlik geskik vir ons om te ploeg. We were very happy when we got the place, Platfontein. And we had hoped because our people’s history tells that we live from farming, that this land, which was open and dry, would be a good place for us to cultivate. GOVAN WHITTLES: On farmland meant to preserve their culture, Markus shows us a lake that has formed here over the past seven years. At first, it appears to be a serene stretch of water until he tells us it’s a dam entirely filled with sewage, dumped here by the Sol Plaatje Municipality. GOVAN WHITTLES: I’ve covered sewage in the streets all over the country and I’ve seen what dilapidated sewage plants looks like, but this is unlike anything I’ve ever seen. GOVAN WHITTLES: And it keeps expanding, yet Platfontein doesn’t even have a sewage network. MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons wat nie dienste kry nie, ons wat nie flush toilette het nie, hoekom sal rioolwater by onse plaas gegooi word? We’re the ones who don’t get services, who don’t even have flush toilets, so why would sewage be dumped on our land? GOVAN WHITTLES: Markus says they’re treated like the sewage on their land, cast aside by government because of who they are. MARKUS JETEMBO: Die oudtydse regering het mos ons ouers gebruik gemaak om hulle te help veg. Dit is hoekom hierdie SuidAfrika sien vir ons as vreemdelinge en vir ons nie die nodige dienste wil gee nie. The old government used our parents to fight alongside them. That’s why this South Africa sees us as foreigners and doesn’t want to give us the services we need. GOVAN WHITTLES: But the mess on their land isn’t isolated, it’s just a symptom of an entire network in freefall. TUMELO MOSIKARI: This is Goga pumpstation, it’s where the sewage from Galeshewe comes from, Galeshewe, Carter’s glen and all the other high lying areas comes to. VO: In Galeshewe, Kimberley’s largest township, activist Tumelo Mosikari visits the pump station often and tells us the pumps haven’t been switched on for a long time. GOVAN WHITTLES: What are we gonna see if we go in here? TUMELO MOSIKARI: A non-functioning pumpstation that has had millions allocated to it’s upgrade. GOVAN WHITTLES: Ok, let me ask first. GOVAN WHITTLES: The supervisor appears from the parking lot, insisting the pumps are working. GOVAN WHITTLES: We just want to see if the pumpstation is working, SHAYLE GREY: Ja, it is working. I just came from there. I just came from there and I switched it off now. Govan: you just switched it off now? SHAYLE GREY: I’m actually on my way to go start it again. GOVAN WHITTLES: Inside, the only sign of repair or maintenance we see is a few railings being painted. SHAYLE GREY There was a lot of stories you know that you can venture into and stuff like that, there was complications at Goga pumpstation, but we fixed it. GOVAN WHITTLES: Inside the main system where raw sewage is meant to be pumped out, it’s clear nothing’s working; the water lies still, and one pump is missing. The pump is switched on while we film. But less than ten minutes later, it’s switched off again. Construction work on the pipeline is given as the reason for the sudden shutdown. GOVAN WHITTLES: Shayle has just switched the pump off and now this plant is back to not working. It’s clear they only switched it on for us. GOVAN WHITTLES: We know the only reason they switched it off so quickly was to keep us from seeing it bubbling out, just beyond the wall, in an open field next to the station. GOVAN WHITTLES: have you ever seen anything like this, a sewage river, a manmade sewage river, with banks. TUMELO MOSIKARI: No, and this is normal, this is not something that happened last year. This is pre-2018. In 2018 there was a 30 million Rand project to upgrade the facility. GOVAN WHITTLES: and where did that money go? TUMELO MOSIKARI: Probably down the drain as well. GOVAN WHITTLES: Has this sewage river ever stopped running since 2018? TUMELO MOSIKARI: No, it’s never stopped running, if it had stopped running there wouldn’t be a lake. VO: The sewage river runs for several kilometres and then passes under a provincial road to finally end up in Platfontein. Last year, we reported how the provincial government spent 30 million Rand to raise a part of this road over the sewage instead of fixing the problem. GOVAN WHITTLES: This place is appropriately called the Zamani Soul sewage lake, because this will be the premier’s legacy. It’s a monument of disgust and dysfunction. JOSEF KAJANGA: Die provinsiale regering sê daar is nie geld genoeg om vir julle spoeltoilette te kan maak nie. Daar is nie geld om vir julle die krag te kan aanlê nie om vir julle die waterlyn te kan aanlê nie. The provincial government says there isn’t enough money to give you flush toilets. There’s no money to bring you electricity, or to install water lines. MARKUS JETEMBO: Ek het self by die human rights commission gaan complain oor die feit dat die munisipalteit vir ons bill maar ons kry nie enige diens van die munisipalteit by ons nie. I personally went to the Human Rights Commission to complain about the fact that the municipality bills us, but we don’t receive any services from them. GOVAN WHITTLES: The municipality struggled to explain why Platfontein is being billed at all. SOL PLAATJE: “Im not 100% sure, because from my understanding, there is toilets, which means they are getting water from us, so that means we must bill them” MARKUS JETEMBO : Ons het nie flush toilette nie. We don’t have flush toilets GOVAN WHITTLES: Hulle sê julle het. They say you do. MARKUS JETEMBO : Julle sal net droog saksisteme kry by ons. You’ll only find dry bagging systems here. GOVAN WHITTLES: When the Human Rights Commission pressed the municipal leadership for answers, they were left dumbstruck, unable to explain even the basics. UPSOUND SOL PLAATJE: We cant drink water from the tap is that the question, maybe I misunderstood the questions, maybe I’ll give the question to someone ELSBETH KHWINANA: COMMISSIONER: You don’t even understand why you are in that seat. DR HENK BOSHOFF: This session was an embarrassment for the Sol Plaatje municipality. It is clear that its administration does not know what to do. GOVAN WHITTLES: The commission will push for the report to reach Parliament, something the Khwe hope will finally see them recognised. MARKUS JETEMBO: Ons is mense wat nou nog met ons tradisie sit en ons tradisie praktiseer. Hoe gaan ons ons Vryheid geniet? Ons voel nie deel van SuidAfrika nie, ons voel geïsoleerd. We are people who still practice our traditions. How will we enjoy our freedom. We don’t feel part of South Africa, we feel isolated LINKS AND PROMOS PRESENTER LINK SOURCE: A002C023_251015OF This is a lake on the doorstep of an indigenous community just outside Kimberley. You may think that they live off this water, but the truth is disgustingly different. SOURCE: A002C025_25101589 AFRIKAANS Die lyk dalk soos ‘n mooi dam wat gebruik word deur inheemse mense hier in die Noord-Kaap, maar wat dit regtig is, is ‘n morsige realiteit. MARKUS JETEMBO SOURCE: A002C008_25101570 00:06:53:19 Dis baie morsig, mens raak sommer naar van daai reuk want as jy die omgewing binnegaan, dan kry jy die reuk. MARKUS JETEMBO SOURCE: A002C008_25101570 00:08:19:35 Miskien as die vloei van die rioolwater by goga pompstasie gestopsit word, dit kan miskien 5 tot 10 jaar lê, voordat dit opdroog. Maar daai is ‘n vraag wat ek nie ‘n Antwoord voor het nie, want die ding het klaar verander in ‘n rivier. TUMELO MOSIKARI SOURCE: A002C001_251015FD 00:01:01:29 Raw sewage is coming from the community, its supposed to be pumped to where its treated, its not being treated. Instead of pumping it here they have opened a manhole in the veld to let the raw sewage out. This raw sewage created a lake in Platfontein next to the R31. TUMELO MOSIKARI SOURCE: A003C036_2510155Q 00:08:14:46 There is no action, it is like we don’t have a municipality. 00:08:26:31 They work here, they get paid to make sure that this doesn’t happen and it has been happening for years. TIMELINE PROMOS PROMO 1 VO In Kimberley, one of South Africa’s last indigenous communities finds itself at odds with the municipality, fighting not just neglect, but erasure. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A year after the Premier’s billion-rand promise, the people of the Northern Cape are still waiting no houses, no hope, just politics built on empty ground.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Before the elections, the ANC promised change again but in the Northern Cape, not a single brick has been laid, and the only thing still standing are the lies.
metadata.Summary: In April 2024, Carte Blanche visited the Northern Cape to investigate broken infrastructure and undelivered promises in towns across the province. Among the voices that defined that story was Nellie Frans, a 55-year resident of a shanty settlement outside Kimberley, who told us she had been waiting her entire life for a proper home. During that interview, we confronted Premier Zamani Saul about the stalled R1 billion housing project announced only months earlier. Standing on a sewage-drenched street, he assured Carte Blanche that “by the end of the month, a contractor will be putting up site there.” Eighteen months later, nothing has happened. The community says no contractor ever arrived, no foundations have been dug, and no houses are planned for the site where the Premier made his pledge. Residents claim that the few housing allocations that have gone ahead in Leratoville have been politically selective — allegedly limited to ANC-aligned individuals — and that the newly built houses there are structurally unsound, with cracks, collapsing walls, and poor finishes. For people like Nellie Frans, who once believed that promise might finally bring change, the disillusionment has deepened.

For people like Nellie Frans, who once believed that promise might finally bring change, the disillusionment has deepened. ⸻ STORY FOCUS / ANGLE The follow-up revisits Nellie and her community to ask one simple question: Did the Premier keep his promise? We return to the site where the R1 billion housing project was unveiled to find out: • Has construction begun? • Were tenders issued or funds allocated? • Who, if anyone, received houses? • Are housing allocations being politicised? • And what has become of the Premier’s public assurance that “by the end of the month” work would start?
